newsitem.title: INDIA: Mother Teresa weak, quiet anniversary planned.
newsitem.headline: Mother Teresa weak, quiet anniversary planned.

text.p: Nuns from Mother Teresa's religious order have decided to celebrate the 50th anniversary of its founding next Tuesday in low key because she is still feeble after her release from hospital.

"Although Mother is much better now, she is still very weak and we have decided to celebrate the 50 years of Inspiration without any fanfare," a senior sister from the Roman Catholic Missionaries of Charity, based in Calcutta, said on Sunday.

September 10, 1946, was Mother Teresa's "Inspiration Day" when, she later said, she received direction from God to work for the poor and destitute while travelling by train between Calcutta and the Indian hill-station of Darjeeling.

Mother Teresa, 86, a Nobel Peace laureate known as the Saint of the Gutters for her work with the poor, was released from a Calcutta nursing home on Friday after an 18-day battle against heart problems, malaria and mild pneumonia.
For much of the time Mother Teresa, fitted with a cardiac pacemaker in 1989, was in intensive care and doctors said she suffered two heart attacks.
Mother Teresa spent the weekend resting in her room in the Mother House, the Charity's headquarters in central Calcutta.
Sisters said her poor health had forced them to rule out any extravagant celebration for the 50th anniversary, a day normally marked with balloons, cakes and mini-plays, as well as prayers.
"We will hold mass in all homes and establishments of the Missionaries of Charity all over the world on that day," one sister said.
Sisters of the order view the anniversaries as a time when they rededicate themselves to the poor.
Mother Teresa has described her inspiration to help the poor as "a call within a call... the message was clear. I was to leave the convent and help the poor, while living among them".

The Missionaries of Charity, founded in 1949, runs some 544 homes for unwanted children and the destitute in more than 80 cities. The work includes the care of nearly 7,000 children in 120 homes and arranging 1,500 adoptions each year.
